You previously formulated the following research problem for the target paper.

Research problem: Can MVFA's multi-level residual adapters be trained for cross-modality zero-shot medical anomaly detection and segmentation using only image-level normal/abnormal labels on the source modalities, instead of the pixel-level masks required by its Dice, Focal and BCE alignment losses — and how much of the fully mask-supervised zero-shot performance is retained? Concretely, the problem is to design an image-level-supervised adaptation objective for the four adapter stages of CLIP ViT-L/14 (for example, multiple-instance pooling of the patch-to-text similarity maps at each level, so that an abnormal image must contain at least some highly abnormal patches and a normal image must contain none), train it on the BMAD source modalities with all masks discarded, and measure image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and PRO on each held-out modality under the modality-disjoint leave-one-modality-out protocol, reporting the ratio to mask-supervised MVFA trained on the same splits.
Rationale: MVFA's zero-shot result is obtained by training the adapters with dense, expert-drawn anomaly masks on the source datasets (limitation G3), and its few-shot variant additionally needs labelled abnormal target images (G4). In clinical practice, image-level labels (normal versus abnormal study) are far cheaper and available at scale from reports, whereas pixel masks are rare. The related work shows the field moving in the opposite direction: MedSAD-CLIP and MLCA (Fine-Tuning CLIP with Convolutional Features) both keep or strengthen pixel-level supervision, AnomalyCLIP and AdaCLIP-style prompt learners are trained on auxiliary data with masks, and only training-free methods such as AnoCLIP and SAA+ avoid masks, at a large cost in localisation accuracy. Whether multi-level visual adaptation can be learned from weak labels — and whether localisation emerges from image-level supervision through the patch-text similarity maps — is therefore unanswered, and the answer decides whether MVFA-style adaptation is usable when masks do not exist. The question is narrow (it changes only the training signal of one component, the adapter alignment loss), directly implementable in the public MVFA code by replacing the loss on the patch similarity maps, and measurable on BMAD with one GPU. Evaluating it under the modality-disjoint protocol (RESC and OCT17 held out together) ensures that any retained performance reflects genuine transfer to unseen modalities rather than leakage between the two retinal OCT datasets.

ReviewingAgents evaluated it on five criteria. Their reviews, feedback, and ratings are:
- Clarity: rating 4/5. Review: The problem names the exact component (the alignment loss of the four adapter stages), the change (image-level labels only, masks discarded), the setting (zero-shot, leave-one-modality-out on BMAD) and the outcomes (image AUROC, pixel AUROC, PRO, retention ratio versus mask-supervised MVFA). The scope and boundaries are easy to grasp. Feedback: Fix the mechanism less loosely: 'for example, multiple-instance pooling' leaves open whether the study is about MIL specifically or about any weak-label objective. State the primary pooling operator (e.g., top-k mean of patch scores) and treat others as ablations. Also specify which BMAD source datasets actually have image-level labels for both classes in their training split.
- Relevance: rating 5/5. Review: Annotation cost is the central obstacle named in the target paper's own motivation and in most related medical works (MedicalCLIP, MedCLIP-SAMv2, MadCLIP). The problem builds directly on MVFA's architecture and benchmark and asks a question the field has avoided: recent follow-ups (MedSAD-CLIP, MLCA) increase rather than decrease pixel supervision. Feedback: Make the connection to weakly-supervised segmentation literature explicit so that the contribution is positioned as transferring weak supervision to multi-level VLM adaptation rather than inventing weak supervision.
- Originality: rating 3/5. Review: Learning localisation from image-level labels is well established outside this area (multiple-instance learning, class-activation-map based weakly supervised segmentation, MIL in video anomaly detection). What is new is applying it to the patch-to-text similarity maps of a multi-level CLIP adapter and testing whether the resulting localisation transfers to unseen modalities. That is a moderately novel combination rather than a new challenge. Feedback: Sharpen the novel element: for instance, ask whether text-anchored patch similarities make MIL localisation transfer better than visual-only MIL, or whether multi-level supervision changes where localisation emerges. Without such a hook the problem risks reading as 'MIL applied to MVFA'.
- Feasibility: rating 5/5. Review: Highly feasible: the change is a loss replacement in public code, BMAD provides image-level labels for every dataset, training cost equals MVFA's (which ran on one RTX 3090), and the evaluation reuses MVFA's metrics. The only risk is that MIL training collapses to trivial maps, which is itself a measurable outcome. Feedback: Plan a short pilot on a single held-out modality to verify that the weak loss produces non-trivial maps before running all six leave-one-out folds and three seeds.
- Significance: rating 4/5. Review: If a large fraction of mask-supervised zero-shot performance can be retained from image-level labels, MVFA-style adaptation becomes trainable on report-labelled hospital data, which substantially widens its practical applicability. A negative result is also informative because it quantifies the value of masks. Feedback: Strengthen significance by also measuring what happens when image-labelled data is plentiful (more images without masks versus fewer images with masks), which is the realistic trade-off for clinical sites.

Revise the research problem so that it addresses the feedback while keeping what the reviewers rated highly. Keep it a single, fine-grained, to-the-point problem that still addresses the same limitations, respects the constraints below, and stays centred on the target paper.

Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- G3. Annotation requirements remain clinically heavy: The adaptation objective is trained on pixel-level anomaly-segmentation masks using a combination of Dice, Focal, and binary cross-entropy losses across four feature levels, including under zero-shot evaluation. This effectively requires dense expert annotation for every training image; the method does not formulate an image-level-only, sparse, or normal-only supervision variant, which weakens its relevance to label-scarce clinical settings.
- G4. The few-shot setting is underspecified and operationally costly: The K annotated target images must simultaneously supply normal exemplars for the memory bank and abnormal examples for adapter training, yet the partition between the two is left unspecified; for K = 2 this may be infeasible if sufficient exemplars of both classes are required. Clinical few-shot supervision, in practice, may contain only normal or entirely unlabeled data. The method further implies per-task retraining, yet training time and computational cost are not reported.
Constraints:
- The problem will be investigated by a student team in the next few weeks by modifying the public code of the target paper (https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD) and evaluating on the public BMAD benchmark (brain MRI, liver CT, retinal OCT: RESC and OCT17, chest X-ray, histopathology), using a single Google Colab Pro GPU (A100 40GB or L4 24GB). No new clinical data can be collected and no new expert annotations can be made.
- Shared evaluation protocol (from limitation group C: G2, G10, G12): results must be reported under a modality-disjoint leave-one-modality-out split (RESC and OCT17 are held out together, never one with the other in training), with patient-level separation where identifiers exist, over at least 3 random seeds and 3 few-shot support draws with mean and standard deviation, and against the missing baselines named in G12 where relevant.

Problem: In BMAD, pixel-level masks exist only for brain MRI, liver CT and RESC, while OCT17, chest X-ray and histopathology carry image-level labels only, so MVFA's mask-based multi-level alignment loss can learn from just half of its potential source data. Can MVFA's four adapter stages instead be trained with an image-level multiple-instance objective on the patch-to-text similarity maps — primary operator: top-k mean pooling of each level's patch anomaly scores, so an abnormal image must contain a small set of highly abnormal patches and a normal image none — using all source datasets with masks discarded, and (i) how much zero-shot image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and PRO on the held-out modality is retained relative to mask-supervised MVFA, (ii) at which of the four feature levels localisation emerges under image-level supervision, and (iii) whether adding image-labelled-only datasets to the source pool compensates for the loss of masks? All results under the modality-disjoint leave-one-modality-out protocol with 3 seeds.

Rationale: The reviewers asked for a sharper novel element and a realistic trade-off. The novel element is twofold: the weak signal acts on text-anchored patch similarities at multiple ViT depths, which is not how weakly supervised segmentation is usually done (single-level class-activation maps), and it lets MVFA use source datasets that its current loss simply ignores. The label-budget question (iii) — more images with image labels versus fewer images with masks — is the decision a clinical site actually faces. The mechanism is fixed (top-k mean; max pooling and attention-MIL become ablations), the component is a single loss in the public MVFA code, and the evaluation reuses MVFA's metrics on BMAD under the shared modality-disjoint, multi-seed protocol, which keeps the problem feasible on one GPU. A negative result is still informative because it quantifies what pixel masks buy for cross-modality transfer.
